title: candidate-scratchpad-maya-chang-runtime-lead
content:
Quick scratchpad after interviews w/ Maya Chang (candidate) for Runtime Lead role. Informal notes — meant for internal debrief + my memory. Will clean up if we move to panel debrief.

Context: 5–7y infra+inference ops with strong MLOps orientation. Current: Senior Infra Engineer @ CloudSynth (focused on inference infra, some model onboarding). Applying for Runtime Lead (serving runtime) — role would own kernel selection heuristics, batching, and onboarding process for new open models.

Interviewers:
- Me (Maya Chang) — hiring interviewer (system design + inference ops)
- Aisha Rahman — latency/throughput measurements, benchmarking
- Connor Lee — team fit, leadership, incident response

Rounds covered today (60m total):
1) 15m intro / background / role clarifying questions
2) 20m system design: high-throughput KV-caching + fallback for model variants
3) 15m technical deep dive: quantization tradeoffs + kernel selection heuristics
4) 10m behavioral / leadership / ambiguity

High-level impression (speed-read):
- Solid practical background — has shipped caching+batching system at previous orgs, pragmatic about tradeoffs.
- Communication: concise, uses diagrams when prompted, good at clarifying assumptions early.
- Weakness: limited exposure to GPU kernel tuning (CUDA-level), most experience was at higher abstraction (operator-level, inference orchestration). Comfortable driving spec with FPGA/TPU? less so.

Detailed notes (by section):
Intro/background:
- Came from a small infra team (5) — led efforts to roll out model serving across several teams (text + vision). Focus was on reliability and cost.
- Mentions implementing an LRU-ish prefix cache for transformer KV that reduced token compute by ~22% on average for synchronous pipelines.
- Has metrics around cost savings, but not attached to per-token numbers; says "reduced infra spend" by ~20% without giving absolute baseline. TODO: ask finance for relative baseline if we progress.

System design (KV-caching + fallback):
- Proposed architecture: deterministic sharding of cache keys by model+customer, TTL + eviction policy based on request frequency, separate hot-path in-memory store (redis-like) with async persistence to s3 for long-term cache.
- Likes idea of automated cache priming for common prefixes (proactive warmup). Suggests offline job to compute hot prefixes from request logs — reasonable.
- Fallback policy: suggested tiered fallback from exact model -> lower-quality quantized variant -> CPU fallback using smaller model. Good alignment with our graceful degradation story.
- Missed: didn't propose metrics to track cache effectiveness beyond hit rate (e.g., tail latency impact, cost delta correlated to tokens saved). I prompted and they recovered with suggestions (p95 latency with/without cache, tokens_saved per minute).

Technical deep dive (quantization & kernels):
- Understands quantization tradeoffs (int8 vs int4) and that model architecture + activation distribution matters. Provided lucid examples of where per-layer quantization hurts.
- Noted that kernel selection should be dynamic based on sequence length distribution — suggested profiling histograms and picking kernels per-shape at deploy time. This is aligned w/ our compilation strategy.
- Gap: limited low-level exposure to CUDA optimization; hasn’t implemented custom kernels; mostly relied on vendor libraries and tuned operator fusion. Said they'd be comfortable collaborating with an applied-kernels engineer.

Leadership & incident response:
- Described an incident where auto-scaler misestimated growth and caused cascading queueing. Candidate led postmortem, created a runbook and a new autoscaler heuristic. Shows good ownership.
- Thinks in terms of SLAs and operational runbooks; emphasizes blameless postmortems and synthetic traffic tests.

Red flags / risks:
- Low exposure to writing GPU kernels — might need to pair w/ lower-latency team on perf-critical stack. Not a dealbreaker; could own orchestration/heuristics.
- Has preferences for certain OSS (prefers their in-house redis variant) — may require some persuasion when we standardize on components.
- Sample size at previous company small; unsure about scaling across hundreds of tenants simultaneously.

Strengths / positives:
- Pragmatic tradeoff reasoning (latency vs cost) and can tie proposals to measurable metrics.
- Good sense of rollout strategies (canary, shadow, gradual traffic ramp).
- Clear expectation management — says "we'll aim for p95 SLA within 6 weeks" rather than overly optimistic pledges.

Scorecard (rough, 1–5):
- System design: 4
- Low-level performance / kernel expertise: 3
- Inference domain knowledge (KV cache, batching, quantization): 4
- Ownership & leadership: 4
- Communication: 4
- Culture fit: 4
Overall: 3.8 (lean hire for a role that prioritizes orchestration/ownership; borderline if we require deep kernel engineering immediately)

Suggested next steps:
- Optional follow-up: pair session with a senior kernels engineer (30–45m) to probe CUDA/kernel-level comfort. Important if we prioritize kernel ownership.
- Ask for a short writeup: design a rollout plan for adding a quantized variant to a production model with metrics and rollback criteria (1–2 pages). Good for assessing operational rigor.
- Compensation expectations: asked about range; candidate expects at least upper-mid range for IC4/IC5. Need to confirm against comp bands.

Unresolved questions (write down for panel):
- How comfortable are they reading/iterating on CUDA code? Can they debug kernel-level regressions in flames?
- Concrete numbers: per-token savings claim needs baseline (we should request context).
- Can they lead hiring for a 2–3 person team? Past org was small; get more examples of recruiting/mentoring.

Notes to self (Maya):
- Bring up during debrief: candidate seems like a good complement if we split kernel ownership vs runtime orchestration across two hires.
- If we want a single-hire solution who can do both, this candidate might need additional ramp or we favor someone with deeper CUDA background.
- Flag for Aisha to validate quantization claims against our benchmark harness (run candidate-provided patch or pseudo-experiments)

If we progress: items to ask HR / recruiting:
- Confirm notice period and earliest start date. Candidate mentioned 6–8 weeks preferred.
- Check references focusing on kernel debugging and scale experience (ask "did they own perf regressions end-to-end?").

Raw transcript fragments (for memory):
- "We used a mix of heuristics and offline profiling to pick kernels by shape — not perfect but gave us 12–18% speedup on medium-length sequences."
- "I prefer to ship something measurable fast and iterate — not perfect from day one."

End scratchpad. Will convert this into a tidy panel scorecard if we decide to move to onsite.
